summary: Introductory hosted API demo focused on chat/generation basics: streaming behavior, key generation params, and practical retry/backoff patterns. Customer is evaluating for patient-facing messaging; security and latency are top concerns.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Alright hi everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood Inference, I'm the AE on this account. we also have Arjun our solutions engineer. Quick intros?
[00:08] Sofia: Hi this is Sofia, product at LumosHealth, I'm leading the chat bot initiative.
[00:12] Ben: Ben here, eng lead. we own the backend integrations.
[00:15] Dana: Dana, CTO. I'm mainly here to hear about security and latency.
[00:20] Arjun: Great, quick agenda: short hosted API demo for chat/generation, show streaming behavior live, go over params and then retry/backoff patterns and a short Console tour for observability.
[00:30] Sofia: Perfect. Our big asks: patient PII, sub-200ms median latency target on short queries, and predictable cost.
[00:37] Maya: noted. we'll try to address those as we go.
[00:45] [demo start — screen shared]
[00:48] Arjun: I'm starting with a simple POST to /v1/chat generate. Model in this demo is a smaller open variant we keep in catalog — for demo I picked redwood-feather-7b (note: model names in transcript might be fuzzy).
[01:05] Arjun: Observe streaming: we open an SSE-like stream, server sends partial token chunks, the client can render incremental text. this helps perceived latency because tokens appear earlier.
[01:22] Ben: Is streaming safe for our mobile clients? we worry about intermittent networks.
[01:26] Arjun: Yes, but you need to handle reconnects and idempotency. recommended pattern: include a client_message_id or conversation_id and sequence offsets. if a stream disconnects, you retry with exponential backoff and resume if you have the last token index. otherwise you re-request final generation and dedupe on the client if duplicates appear.
[01:50] Sofia: How verbose are partial tokens — like do we get punctuation broken mid-word?
[01:54] Arjun: Sometimes. streaming sends token pieces so you may see incomplete words. UX trick: buffer a few tokens (200ms) before flashing to the user, or show a typing indicator while tokens trickle. also we can choose between chunked vs SSE.
[02:10] [Speaker 2]: (mumble) we've seen browsers close connections at 30s.
[02:15] Arjun: right, which is why we suggest short keepalive heartbeats and fallbacks. if you need long polling for long-form generation, we support async jobs too — /v1/jobs endpoint for longer outputs.
[02:32] Dana: On security — how do you handle PHI? encryption, audit?
[02:36] Maya: we offer TLS in transit, KMS integrations for key management for Private deployments, and the hosted plane stores minimal data by default — retention configurable. We'll send the security whitepaper and SOC2 docs.
[02:50] Ben: For retries, are you saying re-issuing the same request could double-bill tokens? that's a concern.
[02:56] Arjun: It can if you re-run full generation. strategies: 1) make operations idempotent with a dedupe key server-side, 2) implement short response caching (prefix/K V cache) for recent turns so retries hit cache not generation, 3) prefer resume semantics where feasible. Redwood also offers token accounting in Console so you can spot retry storms.
[03:20] Sofia: Could you show param tuning — like temperature and top_p — with an example?
[03:25] Arjun: Sure. I'll change temperature from 0.7 to 0.2; you can see outputs become more deterministic. in the demo request body I also lowered max_tokens to 120 for chat responses to keep cost down and latency predictable.
[03:42] [00:03:42 timestamp glitch, auto caption error]
[03:45] Arjun: Also show top_p set to 0.9 for a medium diversity. For patient messaging where hallucination is risky, we recommend lower temp (0.0-0.3), top_p around 0.8-1.0 and also strong system prompts / constraint templates.
[04:05] Ben: Do you provide tools for prompt testing?
[04:08] Arjun: Yes, Console has a prompt playground and Optimize will run a small evaluation set and suggest quantization or model changes for cost/latency improvements. we'll demo that after the call if you want.
[04:22] Sofia: We need to keep latency around 150-200ms for short queries — what model would you recommend hosted vs dedicated?
[04:31] Maya: For that latency and production scale, likely dedicated GPU pools. For initial POC, hosted with a smaller low-latency model might suffice; Redwood can route to lower-latency variants. Decision depends on throughput.
[04:45] Arjun: Also batching affects tail latency. continuous batching yields lower unit cost but increases latency variability. you can set batch windows and max latency thresholds in the runtime config.
[05:00] Ben: Example of a retry/backoff we should implement?
[05:03] Arjun: exponential backoff with full jitter: initial 200ms, multiply by 2 up to a cap ~5s, add jitter. Only retry on idempotent-safe errors — 429/5xx/connection reset — not on 400-level input errors. implement an overall retry budget per request (e.g., 3 retries) and track risk of duplicated tokens.
[05:26] Sofia: what's the best way to surface partial content to avoid duplication?
[05:29] Arjun: have server-side message ids and sequence numbers in stream frames. client can assemble, and when you retry, ask for resume starting at sequence N. if resume isn't supported, do cached lookup. if neither, re-gen but compare checksum of last N tokens and dedupe on client.
[05:48] [Pause, demo switches to Console]
[05:52] Arjun: quick Console tour: per-route token breakdown, per-model latency percentiles, and a trace view for each request. you can filter by token cost, model, or route.
[06:10] Dana: Will those logs contain PII? we need controls.
[06:13] Maya: Logs are redact-able and retention is configurable; we can set zero-retention for sensitive customers and provide audit exports.
[06:24] Ben: about cost: how do we estimate monthly bills?
[06:27] Maya: Console shows projected spend based on token usage. for streaming, we count generated + prompt tokens. also Optimize can suggest quantization or smaller model to save 30-60% depending on workload.
[06:41] Sofia: any recommended defaults for retries and streaming for mobile clients?
[06:45] Arjun: Yes: keep streaming chunk size small (like 64 tokens max per chunk), show typing UI, buffer 150-300ms, retry with exponential backoff on network errors, and implement resumable ids. For mobile specifically, shorter request timeouts and fallback to non-streaming small responses to avoid partial UI states.
[07:06] Ben: Can we run a short synthetic benchmark with our payloads?
[07:09] Maya: absolutely, that's typically the POC. we'll need your sample prompts, typical concurrency, and latency targets. Arjun will run a baseline on hosted and estimate Dedicated capacity.
[07:21] Arjun: small note on tokenization — for certain languages token counts vary. be conservative on max_tokens. and if you use long messages, consider streaming with partial compress or summary-of-history approach to keep context small.
[07:38] Sofia: You mentioned KV cache — is that the same as prefix caching?
[07:41] Arjun: Related: KV cache stores attention keys/values for a session so repeated prefixes re-use compute. prefix cache stores full generated text for repeated prompts. both reduce cost and latency. Redwood can enable short TTL caches at the shard level.
[07:55] Dana: Are there SLA guarantees for hosted?
[07:58] Maya: Hosted has best-effort. Dedicated comes with SLA options. for regulated workloads we recommend Private or Dedicated for stronger uptime/latency guarantees.
[08:10] [10 minute mark — skipped forward in transcript for clarity]
[10:05] Arjun: demoing a simulated disconnect: I kill network, reconnect, send client_message_id and the server responds with resume tokens — demo shows minimal duplicate content. note: some client SDKs we provide already handle this logic.
[10:30] Ben: Do we need to implement server-side dedupe if we use Redwood SDK?
[10:33] Arjun: SDKs reduce effort but we still recommend server-side dedupe for safety; SDKs manage sequence and resume but your backend should handle idempotent application of messages.
[11:00] Sofia: are there prebuilt compliance artefacts?
[11:03] Maya: yes we'll attach a compliance pack (SOC2, encryption details, subprocessor list).
[11:10] Dana: for POC timeline, we want 3 week evaluation with perf gates — can you commit to running a baseline within 5 business days?
[11:19] Maya: yes, if you share traffic samples and auth we can start within 5 business days.
[11:25] Arjun: one more tip on retries: when you retry after a 5xx, include a header like X-Request-Id from client to server to correlate logs; Console will show both attempts grouped for debugging.
[11:40] Ben: perfect. about model selection: is there an API param to prefer lower-latency variants?
[11:45] Arjun: we have model_alias or performance_tier param; you can request e.g., "latency:low" and the routing layer will prefer smaller variants or local region. also fallback policies if chosen model is unavailable.
[12:02] Sofia: what's the recommended max_tokens for short patient replies?
[12:06] Arjun: we suggest 60-150 depending on message. set stop sequences to avoid run-on. also hard token caps to prevent runaway cost.
[12:18] [15 minute mark — customer questions continue]
[15:05] Ben: can you demo a failure pattern — 429s under burst?
[15:10] Arjun: yes — I throttle a path, you see 429 responses; we recommend client-side rate limiter with token bucket, and server returns Retry-After header. react by backing off and queueing small retries. for sustained high throughput you want Dedicated capacity.
[15:35] Sofia: any tips on batching small interactive requests?
[15:39] Arjun: avoid batching interactive chat messages; batching best for high-throughput batched outputs like embeddings. for chat, prefer small batch windows (<=20ms) to control latency.
[15:52] Dana: what about monitoring and alerting?
[15:55] Maya: Console supports alerting on error rates, p50/p95 latency, and cost spikes. you can integrate with PagerDuty and Slack.
[16:10] [Short silence]
[16:15] Sofia: ok recap for us: 1) POC with hosted baseline 2) security docs 3) pricing 4) POC kickoff next week.
[16:22] Maya: correct. I'll send the proposal and pricing. Arjun will get the prompt/payload checklist and perf baseline.
[16:30] Ben: Can you include a small sample SDK snippet for iOS streaming?
[16:34] Arjun: yes, I'll include iOS and Node examples and a short flow for resume semantics.
[16:40] Dana: one last question — if we move to Dedicated later, is migration seamless?
[16:44] Maya: yes, same API and console; routing and model pinning make the migration smooth. there may be a cutover window but we support canaries.
[16:55] Sofia: thanks team, this was helpful.
[17:00] Maya: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the next steps.
[17:05] [call ends — notes]
